title: Stale Statistics & Cardinality Misestimates
description: Out-of-date statistics make the optimizer misestimate rows and pick a bad plan; refreshing them restores a good one. Why it matters: stale statistics are a leading, often-overlooked cause of "it was fine yesterday" performance regressions -- especially on fast-growing tables.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine asking a store manager "about how many red shirts do you have in stock?" and getting an answer based on last year's inventory count. If the store has since sold out of red shirts, or gotten a huge new shipment, that stale answer will lead you to make a bad decision — maybe you tell a customer "sure, we definitely have one" when they're actually all gone. SQL Server's query optimizer relies on its own internal "inventory count" — called statistics — to decide how to run every query, and this lesson is about what happens when that inventory count goes stale.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** Every time the SQL Server optimizer plans how to execute a query, it needs to guess how many rows will match each filter, each join, each step along the way. It doesn't count the actual rows before running the query — that would be too slow to do every time. Instead, it keeps a compact statistical summary of the data in each column (a histogram, roughly: "here's the general shape of the values in this column, and how common each range is"), and uses that summary to estimate row counts without scanning the whole table. Those summaries are called statistics, and this lesson is about what happens when they no longer reflect reality — because the underlying data has changed a lot since the statistics were last refreshed, but nobody told the optimizer.

**Why this happens in real databases.** SQL Server does automatically refresh statistics on its own, but only after enough of the underlying data has changed — a percentage-based threshold, not an instant reaction to every single insert or update. In between those automatic refreshes, especially right after a big bulk load, a large batch delete, or a sudden burst of new data, the stored statistics can be significantly out of date compared to the table's actual current content. The optimizer doesn't know this has happened — it just trusts the statistics it has and estimates accordingly. If those numbers are wrong, everything downstream built on top of that estimate is wrong too.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Here's the chain reaction: the optimizer looks at a filter like `WHERE Status = 'Pending'` and consults the statistics on the `Status` column to estimate "'Pending' currently matches about N rows." Based on that guessed row count, it picks an execution strategy. If N is small, it might choose a nonclustered index seek plus lookups, betting that a handful of targeted reads will be cheap. If N is large, it might instead choose a full scan, betting that reading everything sequentially beats doing thousands of individual lookups. This is a genuine cost trade-off, and which side of it wins depends entirely on how many rows actually match. Now suppose the statistics say "about 200 rows match 'Pending'" because that was true when the statistics were last updated, but in reality, after a recent surge, 200,000 rows now match. The optimizer, trusting its stale number, picks the seek-plus-lookup plan meant for 200 rows — and then the query actually executes against 200,000 rows using that plan, doing hundreds of thousands of individual, expensive lookups instead of one efficient scan. The query doesn't just run a bit slower than ideal — it can run catastrophically slower, because the entire strategy was chosen for a completely different, wrong scale of data.

This is also exactly the same mechanism behind "the query ran instantly yesterday and is timing out today" reports, when nothing in the application code changed at all. The data changed, the statistics didn't keep up, and the optimizer kept confidently executing a plan that made sense for yesterday's data distribution.

**Why this matters in production.** Stale statistics are one of the most common, and most overlooked, causes of sudden and mysterious query slowdowns in real systems — "overlooked" specifically because there's no error message, no broken code, and the query text is completely unchanged. Everything about the situation looks like nothing should be wrong, which is exactly why it confuses people troubleshooting it for the first time. The signal to look for is a mismatch between the optimizer's estimated row count and the actual row count in the execution plan — SQL Server shows both side by side, and a huge gap between "Estimated Number of Rows" and "Actual Number of Rows" on the same operator is the fingerprint of a cardinality misestimate, usually caused by stale (or sometimes simply insufficiently detailed) statistics.

The fix is refreshing the statistics — telling SQL Server to go actually look at the current data and rebuild its summary — after which the optimizer, given accurate numbers, picks the plan that's actually appropriate for the data as it exists right now. This lesson walks through exactly that: a bad estimate producing a bad plan, and an `UPDATE STATISTICS` call restoring the optimizer's ability to make a sensible choice.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below deliberately lets statistics go stale relative to the actual data, then shows you the resulting execution plan side by side with its estimated-versus-actual row counts — look for the gap between what the optimizer expected and what actually happened. After running `UPDATE STATISTICS`, re-run the same query and watch the plan change entirely, now built on numbers that actually match the data currently in the table. This side-by-side comparison is exactly the diagnostic habit worth building: whenever a plan looks like a poor fit for what a query is actually doing, checking the estimated-vs-actual row counts is usually the fastest way to confirm whether stale statistics are the culprit.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** Stale statistics don't only cause the seek-versus-scan misjudgment shown here — the same bad estimate can push the optimizer toward the wrong join type, the wrong join order in a multi-table query, or an undersized memory grant that then causes exactly the kind of tempdb spill covered elsewhere in this course. Whenever a plan looks inexplicably mismatched to what a query is actually doing — wrong join strategy, spilling, or an index being skipped for no obvious reason — checking estimated-versus-actual row counts, and refreshing statistics if they're stale, is one of the cheapest, highest-value diagnostic steps available.

## Scenario
`SELECT CustomerId, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 999` returns ~300k rows but the plan chose an **Index Seek + Key Lookup** (Nested Loops) as if only **one** row matched. It's doing hundreds of thousands of lookups.

## Why it's slow
This is the classic **ascending-key** problem. Statistics were captured when the table only held `CustomerId` values 1–50, so the histogram's maximum key is 50. Then 300k rows for `CustomerId = 999` were loaded, but the histogram was never refreshed (auto-update is off here to simulate a large table past the auto-update threshold). Because 999 sits **beyond the end of the histogram**, the optimizer estimates **~1 row**, picks a seek + per-row lookup, and then actually processes 300k — a catastrophic misestimate.

## What to look for
- A huge gap between **Estimated** (~1) and **Actual** (~300k) rows on the seek.
- A **Nested Loops** plan built for a single row doing **per-row lookups** against the table — watch the logical reads explode into the hundreds of thousands.

## The concept
The optimizer is only as good as its statistics. Values inserted above the histogram's top boundary are invisible to it until stats are refreshed. `UPDATE STATISTICS` rebuilds the histogram; with a correct estimate the optimizer abandons the per-row lookup plan for a set-based scan. On real systems, keep auto-update stats on and/or maintain stats on large, volatile, ever-increasing key columns.
startingQuery: SELECT CustomerId, Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 999 OPTION (USE HINT('FORCE_LEGACY_CARDINALITY_ESTIMATION'));
hints: Compare Estimated vs Actual rows on the operators — how far off is it?
The histogram tops out at CustomerId = 50; value 999 was inserted afterward and sits past the end of the histogram, so it estimates ~1 row.
Run UPDATE STATISTICS Orders WITH FULLSCAN, then re-run the query.
